title: Inspired by a real-life event where drivers fight to park on a moving trailer, I've spent the past 4 weeks building this game with Claude Code
author: OrcGrandma
selftext:
Hi, I'm a game designer at a small indie studio in Korea. Four weeks ago, I came across an event that made me think, "This has to be a game." Drivers try to get their cars up onto a moving trailer and fight to stay on it, and it's been popping up at tracks across the U.S. this year. I saw Hudson Speedway's "King of the Hill" in New Hampshire in a YouTube video and started making a game inspired by it right away. Two weeks later our Steam page went live, and now I'm 4 weeks into development, working with my teammate plus Claude Code and Codex.

On the left is the real event, and on the right is our game. Huge thanks to TBERG MEDIA for letting us use their footage in our promo video.

Get Off My Trailer! is an online physics party brawler. You don't play as a car, you play as a ragdoll human, so you have to steal a car, get it onto the trailer, and keep it there. Crash hard and you get thrown out of the driver's seat. Meanwhile, one player drives the truck pulling the trailer and tries to shake everyone off.

Steam page (Coming Soon). If you like it, a wishlist would mean a lot: [Get Off My Trailer!](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5289530/)

# Where I used AI

* Code: I worked with Claude Code. I used Fable only for early design and Opus for most of the planning, and I ran Sonnet as a subagent for exploration tasks to save tokens. Working from my requests, Claude Code has built (and is still building) much of the game: the Three.js rendering, jointed Rapier ragdolls for the characters, the Electron desktop app, and host-authoritative online play over Steam P2P.
* 10 car models: Instead of modeling them by hand, my teammate and I generated them with Blender Python scripts written with Claude Code. I'm no Blender expert, so this is where Claude Code helped me the most.
* Capsule art and logo: I had Claude Code write a spec, then had Codex generate images from it. Personally, I think Codex is a bit better at image generation, though on ChatGPT Plus I hit the usage limit pretty quickly.

# What AI couldn't do

AI didn't decide what's fun. Claude can run headless bot matches and tell me a round still ends with a winner within 2 minutes, but not how it should feel when a ragdoll goes flying, or whether fighting your way onto the trailer is actually fun. We made those calls by playing it ourselves.

AI also didn't see the multiplayer gotchas coming. For example, initializing the Steam API in Electron's main process got the Steam overlay injected into it, and the app crashed at random, anywhere from 80 seconds to 40 minutes later. We tracked it down from crash dumps, and the fix was to start Steam in a separate Electron utility process that doesn't render anything.

If you've built online multiplayer with AI, what was the bug that took you longest to find? And has anyone else here made a game inspired by a real event? I'll read and reply to every comment.
